# CCP benchmark results

Token estimate: ceil(bytes/4), applied identically to CCP and the baselines. Cost rows assume $3 per million input tokens (illustrative). Baselines are *models* of the conventional approach for each source (see bench/README.md), run against the same data.

## Headline

| Source / task | CCP | Conventional tool | ~Tokens (CCP → conventional) | Calls |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| SQL — a 7-question agent session | 8,750 B | 11.4 KB (naive: 738.2 KB) | 2,188 → 2,919 | 9 / 15 |
| Redis — 50 hashes, 2 fields each | 3,642 B | 13.4 KB | 911 → 3,436 | 1 / 51 |
| WebSocket — report on a 3 s window | 457 B | 165.8 KB | 115 → 42,436 | 1 / 1 |
| Socket.IO — report on a 3 s window | 472 B | 141.0 KB | 118 → 36,087 | 1 / 1 |
| CSV — revenue by region, 200k rows | 598 B | 13.1 MB | 150 → 3,431,422 | 1 / 1 |
| REST API — 100 users, 2 fields | 2,710 B | 140.9 KB | 678 → 36,064 | 1 / 1 |

## 1. SQL servers (MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite)

Dataset: 1,000 users, 3,000 posts, 9,000 comments, 5,000 orders (foreign keys users←posts←comments, users←orders).

**Parity** — 12 queries (filters, nested relations, aggregates, ordering, `_tables`) on SQLite, MariaDB 11 and PostgreSQL 17: **byte-identical on all three**.

### Per-task cost

| Task | CCP | SQL-MCP careful | SQL-MCP naive | Calls (CCP / careful / naive) | Saved vs careful | Saved vs naive |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Point lookup: one user, 2 fields | 270 B | 283 B | 471 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 5% | 43% |
| List 100 users, 2 fields | 2,608 B | 3,405 B | 25,259 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 23% | 90% |
| List 1,000 posts, id+title (big body) | 49,947 B | 57,944 B | 457,635 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 14% | 89% |
| Filter: one author's post titles | 304 B | 316 B | 1,088 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 4% | 72% |
| Nested: user -> posts -> comments | 539 B | 699 B | 2,067 B | 1 / 1 / 3 | 23% | 74% |
| Reverse relation: 50 posts + author name | 3,660 B | 3,654 B | 35,668 B | 1 / 1 / 2 | -0% | 90% |
| Three independent lookups | 1,109 B | 1,571 B | 2,640 B | 1 / 3 / 3 | 29% | 58% |
| Report: revenue by status (5,000 orders) | 587 B | 689 B | 478,432 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 15% | 100% |
| Report: top 10 users by spend | 667 B | 816 B | 231,887 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 18% | 100% |
| Report: channel x status matrix | 1,008 B | 1,220 B | 478,432 B | 1 / 1 / 1 | 17% | 100% |

### A whole agent session

Setup + 7 questions (point, filter, nested, reverse relation, 3 batched lookups, two reports).

| | Bytes | ~Tokens | Round trips | Input cost / 1,000 sessions (@$3/M) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **CCP** | 8,750 | 2,188 | 9 | $6.56 |
| SQL-MCP careful | 11,673 | 2,919 | 15 | $8.76 |
| SQL-MCP naive | 755,898 | 188,975 | 18 | $566.92 |

Saved: **25%** vs careful, **99%** vs naive.

## 2. Redis

Dataset: 2,000 user hashes (8 fields), 500 session strings with TTL, a 300-member leaderboard. Baseline = a conventional per-command Redis tool set (`scan`, `type`, `ttl`, `hgetall`/`hmget`, `info`, `zrange`), one MCP call per command.

| Task | CCP | Baseline (typical) | Baseline (field-aware) | Calls (CCP / baseline) | Saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 user hashes, name+email | 3,642 B | 29,712 B | 13,741 B | 1 / 51 | 88% |
| One hash, 2 fields | 262 B | 573 B | 239 B | 1 / 1 | 54% |
| 100 keys with type + TTL | 4,937 B | 42,225 B | same | 1 / 201 | 88% |
| Memory stats (3 numbers) | 319 B | 1,873 B | same | 1 / 1 | 83% |
| Top-10 leaderboard | 616 B | 482 B | same | 1 / 1 | -28% |

*Typical* = `HGETALL`-style tools returning whole values; *field-aware* = the baseline picks fields with `HMGET`.

### Speed: one pipelined call vs N+1 round trips

Fetching 50 hashes' fields: CCP **0.83 ms** (1 MCP call; to Redis it is 2 round trips: one `SCAN` plus one pipelined batch) vs **14.74 ms** for 50 sequential `HMGET` on localhost alone. Each extra round trip also costs the *network* RTT, so against a remote Redis (modelled, not measured):

| Network RTT | CCP (2 RTT + server) | 51 sequential commands |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5 ms | 1.8 ms | 40.2 ms |
| 2 ms | 4.8 ms | 116.7 ms |
| 10 ms | 20.8 ms | 524.7 ms |
| 50 ms | 100.8 ms | 2564.7 ms |

## 3. Event streams (WebSocket, Socket.IO)

A local feed pushes ~330-byte JSON trades at 200 msg/s (Socket.IO: 80% `trade`, 20% `heartbeat`, Engine.IO v4 framing). The baseline is the usual stream tool: `receive(seconds)` returns every raw message to the model.

| Task | CCP | Raw-stream tool | Saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| WebSocket: Report a 3s window (600 events): count + per-symbol | 457 B | 169,744 B (165.8 KB) | 100% |
| WebSocket: Price min/max/avg over 3s | 303 B | 169,744 B (165.8 KB) | 100% |
| WebSocket: Last 5 trades, symbol + price | 353 B | 1,585 B (1,585 B) | 78% |
| Socket.IO: Report a 3s window (600 events): count + per-symbol | 472 B | 144,345 B (141.0 KB) | 100% |
| Socket.IO: Price min/max/avg over 3s | 321 B | 144,345 B (141.0 KB) | 100% |
| Socket.IO: Last 5 trades, symbol + price | 368 B | 1,644 B (1,644 B) | 78% |

### Reader throughput and query latency

| Server | Ingest (burst of 100k) | Throughput | Reader CPU | RSS after | `messages(limit:20)` p50 / p95 | `summary(field)` on full buffer p50 / p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| websocket-ccp | 100,010 msgs in 0.64s | 155,407 msg/s (38 MB/s) | 0.02s | 8 MB | 0.03 / 0.06 ms | 0.21 / 0.57 ms |
| socketio-ccp | 100,010 msgs in 0.53s | 187,846 msg/s (48 MB/s) | 0.04s | 8 MB | 0.03 / 0.03 ms | 0.32 / 0.54 ms |

The buffer keeps the newest 5,000 messages (32 MB cap), so memory stays flat however long the stream runs; JSON is parsed lazily, only for messages a query actually touches.

## 4. CSV reporting

`sales.csv`: 200,000 rows, 13.1 MB. Baseline = a file-reading tool; the whole file is ≈3,431,422 tokens, far beyond any context window (even a 200-row head costs 14,006 B and answers nothing).

| Task | CCP | Reading the file | Saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue + orders by region (200,000 rows) | 598 B | 13,725,686 B | 100% |
| Top 5 products by quantity (200,000 rows) | 498 B | 13,725,686 B | 100% |
| Region x channel matrix (200,000 rows) | 1,273 B | 13,725,686 B | 100% |
| Distinct customers and overall max price (200,000 rows) | 329 B | 13,725,686 B | 100% |
| 3 priciest APAC app orders | 391 B | 13,725,686 B | 100% |

Load (spawn → ready, parse + type-infer 200,000 rows into memory): **0.71 s**. Aggregate query latency afterwards:

| Query | p50 | p95 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue + orders by region | 62.9 ms | 74.8 ms |
| Top 5 products by quantity | 77.1 ms | 123.0 ms |

## 5. REST / JSON APIs

A local API returns realistic bloated user objects (~2.5 KB each, nested). Baseline = a `fetch(url)` tool that returns the response body.

| Task | CCP | Full response | Saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| One user: name, email, city | 312 B | 1,640 B | 81% |
| One user: just the follower count | 255 B | 1,640 B | 84% |
| List of 100 users: id + name | 2,710 B | 144,255 B | 98% |
| List of 100 users: name + company + city | 7,267 B | 144,255 B | 95% |

Overhead of going through CCP: single-object call **0.21 ms** p50 (incl. MCP round trip) vs **0.16 ms** for a bare HTTP GET from Python on the same machine.

## 6. Footprint and speed

Release builds (LTO, stripped). *Cold start* = spawn → `initialize` + `tools/list` answered, which includes connecting and (for SQL) reading the catalog, (for CSV) loading and type-inferring 200k rows, (for streams) the first handshake. Latency is a typical query measured through the full MCP path (JSON-RPC in/out), 100 runs.
